purpose: Data-driven grammar engine (§29). Six authored concepts, each pointing at a real published lesson. Concept / pattern / examples / exceptions / learner note / common mistakes / level / prerequisite — conservative, checked Hindi, nothing invented.

concepts.concept: Word order — the verb goes last
concepts.pattern: Subject + Object + Verb  (मैं रोटी खाता हूँ)

examples.gloss: I bread eat am — “I eat bread.”
she book reads — “She reads a book.”
we Delhi in live — “We live in Delhi.”

exceptions: Yes/no questions put क्या (kya) at the front: क्या आप अंग्रेज़ी बोलते हैं?
Question words (कहाँ, क्या, कब) sit just before the verb: यह क्या है?
concepts.learnerNote: Hindi is Subject–Object–Verb. The single biggest habit to break is the English Subject–Verb–Object order.
commonMistakes: Copying English order: मैं खाता रोटी
Putting the verb in the middle of the sentence

concepts.concept: Gender — every noun is masculine or feminine
concepts.pattern: -आ (-aa) nouns are usually masculine · -ई (-ii) nouns are usually feminine
exceptions: किताब (kitaab, “book”) is feminine even though it ends in a consonant.
Some -aa nouns are feminine and some -ii nouns are masculine — memorise the exceptions as you meet them.
concepts.learnerNote: Gender controls the adjective and verb forms that agree with the noun, so it has to be learned with every new word.
commonMistakes: Assuming Hindi has no gender because English doesn't
Forgetting that the verb ending changes with the speaker's own gender (मैं जाता हूँ vs मैं जाती हूँ)

concepts.concept: Postpositions — the little words come after the noun
concepts.pattern: noun + postposition (में, से, को, पर, का) — not before
exceptions: का (ka) agrees with the following noun: का / के / की — मेरा घर (my house), मेरी किताब (my book).
concepts.learnerNote: English puts little words before nouns (in, on, for); Hindi puts them after. Postpositions carry most of the grammar of possession and location.
commonMistakes: Saying में दिल्ली (in Delhi) instead of दिल्ली में (Delhi in)
concepts.sourceTitle: Hindi Postpositions — ka, ko, se, meṃ, par

concepts.concept: Verb agreement — the verb matches the subject's gender and number
concepts.pattern: male speaker: -ता (jaata) · female speaker: -ती (jaati) · polite you/they: -ते (jaate)
exceptions: With transitive verbs in the past tense, the -आ ending agrees with the object instead, and the subject takes ने: मैंने रोटी खाई.
concepts.learnerNote: The verb ending changes with who is speaking, not just who is doing the action — a woman says मैं जाती हूँ, a man says मैं जाता हूँ.
commonMistakes: Using the -ता form when a woman is speaking
Forgetting आप always takes the polite plural form आप … हैं
concepts.sourceTitle: Hindi Verbs: Present, Past and Future

exceptions: Masculine consonant-ending nouns take -ों in the oblique plural: लड़कों (ladkon).
Feminine consonant-ending nouns like किताब take -ें: किताबें.
concepts.learnerNote: The plural pattern depends on the noun's gender and ending — learn the pair together (लड़का/लड़के, लड़की/लड़कियाँ).
commonMistakes: Applying the -ए plural to feminine nouns
Using the direct plural where Hindi needs the oblique form (मेरे दोस्तों के साथ)

concepts.pattern: आप (aap) polite · तुम (tum) familiar · तू (tu) intimate — and the verb changes with each

examples.gloss: how are you? — polite, safe with anyone
how are you? — familiar, for friends
how are you? — intimate, only with very close people

exceptions: Using तू with a stranger is genuinely rude; using आप with your own small child is stiff but never wrong.
concepts.learnerNote: When in doubt, use आप. It is never a mistake to be too polite in Hindi.
commonMistakes: Using तुम/तू with elders or strangers
Mixing आप with the तुम verb form (आप … हो is wrong; it is आप … हैं)
concepts.sourceTitle: Aap, Tum or Tu — Getting Politeness Right in Hindi
